transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-06-18 11:00 PT
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Attendees: Mark (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Lucas (Redwood Solutions), James (CTO, Auriga), Sara (Lead Network Eng), Malik (Security Eng), Elena (SRE)

Summary (auto): Initial intake to understand networking constraints for private deployment. Topics: VPC peering vs private endpoints, region gating, egress IPs, latency SLAs, encryption/KMS, audit logs.

[00:00] Mark: hey everyone thanks for carving out time, um i'm Mark from Redwood, i'll kick us off. agenda is to understand your network posture and constraints for a private onramp.
[00:18] James: hey Mark, yeah thanks. we are trying to map out options — we need to run inference in a way that keeps data inside our VPCs and also has predictable egress for firewall rules.
[00:30] Priya: cool, do you have a preferred model of connection—peering, private link, or a transit gateway? or is that what we're trying to decide today?
[00:42] Sara: we mostly prefer peering where possible, but we've got constraints. regional gating is a thing — legal wants eu-only for certain workloads. also we run in aws us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1.
[00:58] Malik: and from security we need KMS integration, HSM support for key material, and audit logs shipped to our splunk. SOC2 is a must.
[01:10] Mark: got it. quick high-level: Redwood supports hosted, dedicated, and private. for private we offer a VPC onramp that can be peered into, or private endpoints (equiv to AWS PrivateLink) where peering is not allowed. both can be restricted by region.
[01:30] Lucas: one nuance — peering gives lower latency and you can do direct routing, but it requires IP planning and routes on your side. private endpoints give a more managed interface but tend to have NAT/egress differences we should call out.
[01:52] Sara: hmm, that NAT thing — can you run through the egress behavior? we need a stable set of source IPs for our firewall, and we can't accept dynamic ephemeral egress coming from hundreds of nodes.
[02:08] Priya: absolutely. for private we can provide static egress IPs per-region for outbound calls to your systems — think of it like a small fleet of NAT gateways managed by Redwood in your private onramp. those are what you would allow in your firewall.
[02:28] James: okay, what's the SLA on those IPs staying stable? we do maintenance windows and IPs must not change without notification.
[02:36] Mark: we can commit to notification and an IP change window. for Dedicated we can reserve persistent NAT egress IPs and put those in the contract; hosted is more dynamic. we'll add that to the checklist.
[02:50] Elena: one question — can the inference traffic stay entirely within the VPC and not traverse public internet?
[02:58] Priya: yes, with peering or private endpoints you can keep traffic on the AWS backbone. the control plane calls to Redwood's management plane may go over the internet unless you opt for a private control plane (available in our Private edition).
[03:18] Malik: private control plane — what does that mean for auditability? we need comprehensive request logs and token-level breakdowns tied to our SSO identities.
[03:28] Lucas: private control plane puts the control plane into your VPC or a customer-managed location. audit logs can be delivered to your S3 or CloudWatch and include token and request-level metadata. small caveat: sampling frequency and retention are configurable — we'll surface defaults and enterprise options.
[03:52] Mark: can i ask about latency goals — what P95 are you targeting for inference?
[04:00] James: we need sub-200ms P95 for our low-latency routing — that's for the 1-2k qps pilot. cost is important but latency wins here.
[04:12] Priya: okay that's helpful. in that range peering to a dedicated pool in-region is usually the best. we can also recommend quantized model variants to get token cost down while preserving latency.
[04:30] Sara: another operational constraint: we operate through a transit gateway and prefer not to create dozens of peering connections. is Redwood able to peer via a transit gateway in each region or use a managed transit model?
[04:42] Priya: yes, we can peer to your transit gateway. we also support a single-entry multi-region model where traffic hits regional onramps that then talk over backbone — depends on your topology. we'll need your TGW account IDs and accepted ASN info.
[05:02] Malik: about encryption — we want BYOK via our KMS and an HSM-backed key. do you support envelope encryption with customer-managed keys?
[05:12] Mark: yes, envelope encryption with customer KMS is supported. for HSM we have integrations with cloud HSMs and can support key material import when you choose private. we'll document the exact key lifecycle steps.
[05:28] James: what's the expected work on our side for setting up peering windows? we usually need network change windows and contact with the vendor's network team.
[05:40] Mark: typical timeline is 1-2 weeks once you schedule the peering window — longest part is firewall approvals. we'll provide Terraform examples and a peering checklist to reduce back-and-forth.
[05:56] Sara: perfect, send the terraform. our change board loves that.
[06:02] Priya: on multi-region routing — do you want active-active in all three regions or primary/secondary failover?
[06:12] James: for phase 1 we want active in us-east-1 and eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1 later. failover must be predictable; we can't have sudden cross-region latency spikes for live traffic.
[06:26] Lucas: two options — active-active with geo-routing and sticky sessions, or active-passive with health-check based failover. active-active needs more cross-region sync and may increase token cost due to cache miss; active-passive is simpler and cheaper but slower on failover.
[06:48] Sara: that cache miss you mentioned — is that KV cache for autoregressive models? we've got prompts that use long histories, so cache reuse matters.
[06:58] Priya: yes KV cache. peering to a local region preserves the KV cache locality. cross-region fallbacks will result in cold KV cache and higher latency/cost. we'll include quantification in the estimate.
[07:18] Malik: any compliance docs available now? we'll need SOC2 type II, ISO 27001, and pen test reports to move forward.
[07:28] Mark: we have a security pack — SOC2 report, ISO cert, pen test summary, and our security whitepaper. i'll send links after this call. note: some specific deployment artifacts for private in your region require a brief NDA amendment, but that's straightforward.
[07:48] James: ok cool. also data residency — certain models will be restricted to eu-west-1 only. can you gate model availability by region?
[07:58] Priya: yes we can pin model serving to regions and enforce region gating in routing. you can also pin specific customers or routes to region-only models.
[08:10] Elena: curious about network egress bandwidth — if we scale to 2k qps in region what egress numbers are we looking at?
[08:18] Priya: it depends on response size, but we'll need to estimate tokens per request. we can produce a bandwidth estimate in the cost/latency doc.
[08:28] Mark: quick note on pricing models — hosted is pay-as-you-go per-token and easiest to start; dedicated is reserved capacity and gives predictable throughput and contract IP guarantees; private includes private control plane and optional on-prem components for air-gapped.
[08:46] James: we lean towards private or dedicated. dedicated if Redwood can colocate a reserved pool for us with steady egress IPs and better price per token.
[08:56] Sara: and operationally we want the ability to rotate keys and have audit logs forwarded. how fast can you spin up a dedicated pool in a new region?
[09:06] Priya: typical lead time is 2-4 weeks for dedicated capacity depending on GPU availability. private control plane usually adds a week.
[09:18] Malik: what about SSO? SAML/SCIM integration for our identity provider, roles, and RBAC?
[09:26] Lucas: supported. we can integrate with your IdP for SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning. RBAC maps to roles and you can have token-level tracing back to identity for audit.
[09:40] James: any precedent for customers who needed HSM + transit gateway + multi-region? curious about complexity.
[09:48] Priya: yes—we recently did a similar setup for a finance customer: transit gateway peering in two regions, private control plane, KMS BYOK with cloud HSM, and audit logs into their SIEM. it was about six weeks from intake to pilot.
[10:06] Sara: great can you share that case study? even anonymized helps.
[10:10] Mark: sure, will add to the follow-up.
[10:16] [Background - brief cross talk planning maintenance window]
[11:00] James: on the firewall side we also need TCP/443 and a couple of outbound webhooks to our internal endpoints — can Redwood call back to our webhooks via the private link?
[11:12] Priya: yes callbacks are possible; we'd want to ensure mutual TLS if you're invoking any internal endpoints. we also support static IPs for webhook egress.
[11:28] Malik: any metrics on RPS per GPU we can expect? we run batch and real-time; batch latency tolerance is higher.
[11:36] Priya: real-time throughput depends on model size and quantization. for example a 7B quantized can do X-requests/sec on A100-ish; we'll produce a table for your workload.
[11:50] Sara: we do have an internal benchmark suite i can share; it's mostly short prompts with a 200 token output.
[11:58] James: timeline — we're aiming to pilot in late july, production in q4. security sign-off is gating.
[12:06] Mark: sounds feasible. action items recap: we'll send peering checklist, terraform snippets, SOC2 and security pack, and latency/cost estimates. you send network diagram and windows.
[12:20] Elena: any non-obvious gotchas we should be aware of when doing peering across accounts and TGWs?
[12:28] Lucas: watch out for overlapping CIDR ranges, route propagation on TGW attachments, and propagation to VPC route tables. also ensure security groups and NACLs allow the flows; we include a checklist to catch those.
[12:46] Malik: last question — for audit retention can you do 13 months or do you have limits?
[12:52] Mark: default retention is 90 days for granular traces, but enterprise plans can extend to 13 or more months. we'll include retention options in the follow-up.
[13:06] James: ok that's everything from me. thanks.
[13:10] Mark: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and estimates. talk soon.
